Iterative Depth-First Search (DFS) is a graph or tree traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each
branch before backtracking, but instead of using recursion, it uses an explicit stack data structure to manage traversal
order. This makes the algorithm iterative in nature, as it avoids relying on the system's call stack.
In traditional DFS, recursion is commonly used to move deeper into the structure, which implicitly makes use of the
call stack to remember the previous states. However, recursion can lead to problems such as stack overflow in deep or
large graphs. The iterative approach solves this problem by replacing the function call stack with a user-defined stack
data structure, which gives more control and safety during traversal.
The algorithm starts by pushing the starting node onto the stack. While the stack is not empty, the algorithm pops the

top node, processes it, and then pushes all
its unvisited neighbors onto the stack. To prevent visiting the same node
multiple times (especially in graphs), a visited set or array is maintained.
